title: When Home Is No Longer There: Adaptation After Forced Migration
summary: Explore the emotional impact of forced migration, from anxiety and grief to loneliness and uncertainty, and how psychological support can help.
body_markdown:
Forced migration is often discussed in terms of safety, documents, housing, work, and other practical challenges. Yet there is another important part of this experience that deserves attention: what happens inside us when we find ourselves in another country not because we had planned to move, but because staying at home became dangerous or impossible. Conversations around World Refugee Day, observed every year on June 20, can help bring attention to these experiences, but the emotional impact of forced migration deserves understanding throughout the year.


There is a big difference between migration that we choose and plan, and forced migration caused by war, danger, or the destruction of home. When we plan to move, even if the process is difficult, there is usually at least some inner readiness. We choose the country, prepare documents, imagine the future, gradually say goodbye to one stage of life and enter another. This kind of migration can also be stressful, but it often contains an important source of support: the feeling of personal choice.


In forced migration, this choice is often absent. We may leave in a hurry, in a state of fear, shock, confusion, and uncertainty. We may leave behind our home, loved ones, work, familiar streets, language, culture, social circle, belongings, and places that had meaning for us. And sometimes there is simply nowhere to return to, because home has been destroyed by war.


This is why adaptation after forced migration can take much longer than we ourselves or the people around us may expect. It cannot be measured by simple phrases such as, “It has been a year, you should be used to it by now,” “You are safe now, why is it still so hard for you?” or “You have housing and work, what else is missing?” These words can be painful because they do not take into account the most important thing: external safety does not always immediately become an inner sense of safety.


We may physically be in a new country, but psychologically remain between two worlds for a long time. One world is the one that existed before the war or before the forced departure. The other is the one in which we have to live now. And between these two worlds there may be a lot of pain, anger, guilt, shame, loneliness, exhaustion, anxiety, longing for home, and a sense of losing control.


Difficulties with adaptation can appear in different ways. We may feel worry, exhaustion, anxiety, fear, irritability, apathy, confusion, sleep problems, tension in the body, emotional numbness, or a feeling that life has been put on pause. It may be difficult to learn a new language, look for work, build new connections, make decisions, feel joy, or plan for the future. All of this is a normal reaction to abnormal circumstances.


Forced migration often becomes a crisis — not only a practical or legal one, but also an inner one. Like any[life transition](https://mindfi.co/blog/navigating-life-transitions) , whether age-related, professional, family-related, or personal, it can raise many questions: Who am I now? Where is my place? What can I rely on? What have I lost? What will happen to me next? Will I be able to feel my life as alive again?


This is why adaptation may not happen quickly. Moreover, we may never fully feel that the new country has become “ours” in the deepest sense. This does not mean that something is wrong with us. It may mean that the losses were very deep, and that the connection with home, language, culture, memories, loved ones, and our previous life remains meaningful.


In a supportive conversation with a specialist, it is not always necessary to look for big solutions immediately. Sometimes the first important step is simply to stop and understand what is happening to you. Why there is so much tiredness, why it is difficult to feel joy, why anxiety does not go away even when things are externally safer. Why a new country may still feel foreign, even after a long time.


The purpose of psychological support is not always to quickly remove anxiety, fear, sadness, or pain. Not all states can simply be “switched off.” And not all feelings need to be fixed. Anxiety, fear, sadness, and uncertainty are part of human life. They may stay with us, especially after experiences of danger, loss, and forced change.


And still, we can learn to live with these experiences in a better way. We can gradually notice them, understand what they are trying to signal, find the nearest sources of support, and regain a greater sense of influence over our own life. Sometimes even the possibility of naming our state and feeling that our experiences matter can bring relief.


In my work, I do not suggest that a person should “adapt faster” or “just move on.” It is important to me to create a space where it is possible to speak honestly about what is happening inside: about tiredness, fear, anger, guilt, shame, confusion, loneliness, or the feeling that life has somehow lost its familiar shape. Without pressure, without devaluation, and without the demand to have answers immediately.


After a forced move, we often have to search again for the shape of our life. Not only to deal with documents, language, work, or new rules, but also to gradually understand how to live after the loss of a familiar world. Sometimes this movement begins not with big decisions, but with very simple things: going for a walk, making one phone call, asking for help, acknowledging our tiredness, missing home, or honestly saying, “It is still hard for me.”


Support from a specialist can be useful precisely when you feel as if you are stuck between survival and life. In such a conversation, it is possible to speak about loss, fear, guilt, anger, shame, exhaustion, and hope. It is possible not to devalue what has been lost, while also gently looking for what can help you endure the present reality.


Such a conversation can be helpful when you need to better understand your current state, see the nearest possible steps, reduce the feeling of loneliness, and feel that your reactions deserve attention rather than a fight against them. Sometimes one supportive meeting can become an important pause: a place where you can slow down, breathe out, and gently notice what needs your attention right now.


If you recognize yourself in this experience, you do not have to make sense of it alone. Together, we can explore what is happening to you now, what exhausts you the most, what you can rely on, and what small steps may help you feel more clarity in your current life.


I would like to remind you: if it is hard for you to adapt after forced migration, it does not mean that you are weak or doing something wrong. Perhaps your psyche is still trying to process too many changes, losses, and uncertainties at the same time.


You do not have to go through this path by yourself. Such a conversation can become a space where your experience is taken seriously, and together with me, you can explore how to live in a new reality with more dignity, attentiveness to yourself, and care for your mental health.


Written by Iryna Melnychenko, Psychotherapist
